metadata.summary: The Roman execution of Jesus that Christians interpret as the climactic atoning death of the Messiah.

evidence_items.claim: Sin-bearing, wounds, healing, shepherd, and guardian images combine scriptural and pastoral language; later atonement theories must identify their additional synthesis.

Ancient background for Atonement includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Leviticus 16:1-34, Isaiah 53:4-12, sacrifice-theme, and leviticus without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Atonement is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.

Ancient background for Christology includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to 2 Samuel 7:8-16, Psalm 2:1-12, messiah-theme, and jesus without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Christology is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.
The execution belongs specifically to Roman imperial punishment while the Gospels interpret it through Israel's scriptural and covenantal categories.
The narratives connect death, shame, kingship, lament, covenant, burial duty, and scriptural interpretation without making Roman execution a Jewish institution.
The crucifixion occurs in first-century Judea under Roman authority and amid Jewish expectations for redemption and deliverance.

Crucifixion displayed Roman coercive power in Judea. The Yehohanan remains show that at least one crucified person later received Jerusalem tomb and ossuary burial, but no single find defines every execution.
Honor and shame patterns appear across ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern societies, especially around kinship, hospitality, public speech, and status.
Scripture recognizes public honor and shame but reorders them under covenant faithfulness, divine vindication, humility, and God's care for the lowly.
Many biblical texts assume group-oriented social worlds where household reputation, public accusation, patronage, and communal recognition mattered deeply.

Second Temple Jewish and Greco-Roman settings used honor, shame, patronage, and public status to frame disputes over authority, purity, discipleship, and crucifixion.

Ancient background for Incarnation includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to 2 Samuel 7:8-16, Psalm 2:1-12, messiah-theme, and christology without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Incarnation is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.

Old Greek Esaias is an ancient Jewish translation and interpretation whose wording sometimes reflects a different Hebrew Vorlage and sometimes the translator's linguistic or theological decisions; New Testament quotations often interact with this Greek tradition.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete sixty-six-chapter witness broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition but containing thousands of orthographic and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and pesharim show active transmission and interpretation.

Responsible interpretation distinguishes a passage's literary sense and historical referent from prediction claims, typology, quotation, allusion, canonical synthesis, Jewish reception, and later christological or ecclesial readings.

Isaiah 52:13-53:12 narrates a servant's humiliation, suffering, death, representative bearing, vindication, and benefit to others, but does not explicitly name the servant; collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and christological readings have long histories.
Mark 10:45 links the Son of Man's service and death with a ransom 'for many'; liberation, Isaiah-servant, martyr, covenant, and atonement readings remain debated.
Royal anointing and kingship were common ancient practices, but the biblical messiah is defined by God’s promise, righteousness, and suffering victory.
Messianic expectation develops from the Davidic covenant, prophetic promise, and the long experience of exile and hope.

Ancient background for Priesthood of Believers includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Leviticus 16:1-34, Isaiah 53:4-12, sacrifice-theme, and atonement without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Priesthood of Believers is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.
Sacrifice was widespread in the ancient world, but Scripture ties it to holiness, covenant access, and God’s redemptive purpose rather than mere appeasement.
Sacrifice joins holiness, atonement, fellowship, and thanksgiving.
Sacrifice runs from early Genesis through Levitical worship and remains central in later prophetic and New Testament reflection.
Temple sacrifice remained a living institution in the Second Temple period and frames the New Testament's sacrificial language.

Ancient background for Suffering Servant Prophecy includes royal courts, sanctuary worship, covenant lawsuits, exile, and restoration hope; the entry ties that world to Isaiah 42:1-9, Isaiah 49:1-7, isaiah, and jesus without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
The servant songs emerge from Isaiah's prophetic world and hold together Israel's vocation, suffering, and restoration.

Ancient background for Theology of Suffering includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Job 1:1-22, Psalm 22:1-31, theology-of-the-cross, and job without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Theology of Suffering is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.

Ancient background for Theology of the Cross includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Job 1:1-22, Psalm 22:1-31, theology-of-suffering, and job without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
Theology of the Cross is read across the canon as Scripture develops this theme from Israel's story into the New Testament witness.
Sacrifices were common across the ancient world, but Israel's system is distinct because the LORD defines the offering, its meaning, and its goal.
